title: First words
goal: Greet people, say yes and no, thank someone and apologise politely in Urdu.
intro:
Urdu conversation starts with greetings, and in Pakistan the universal greeting is **السلام علیکم** (assalāmu ʿalaikum, 'peace be upon you'), used by everyone, everywhere, all day. In this unit you'll learn how to greet and say goodbye, the polite words that make Urdu sound like Urdu — especially the little word **جی** (jī) — and the three words for 'you'.

Don't worry about grammar yet: learn the phrases as whole chunks and practise saying them aloud.

vocab.note: The standard greeting in Pakistan, any time of day. Often shortened to 'salām ʿalaikum'.
Short, friendly. Also 'give my regards': امی کو سلام کہنا.
Traditional Lucknow/Hyderabad greeting, said with a slight raise of the right hand; used across communities in India.
Very common in Pakistan today; means the same as خدا حافظ.
Neutral/informal.
Said alone it means 'yes' or 'pardon?'. Added after names and titles for respect: احمد جی.
f. مہربانی کر کے = please (lit. having done a kindness); آپ کی مہربانی = thank you, that's kind.
Common on signs and in formal requests.
Often pronounced 'māf'. معاف کیجیے = excuse me / sorry.
f. معافی چاہتا ہوں = I apologise (said by a man).
Hugely common: 'achchhā!' = OK! / really? / I see.
ٹھیک ہے = OK, fine.
Default with strangers, elders, anyone you respect. Takes plural verbs.
For friends, younger people, close family.
Only for very close friends, small children, God in prayer — otherwise rude.
Changes for gender/number: کیسا / کیسی / کیسے.
Used, but less common than السلام علیکم in everyday speech.
m. جناب احمد صاحب = Mr Ahmed (very formal).
m. احمد صاحب = Mr Ahmed. For women: صاحبہ sāhiba or بیگم begam.

vocab.note: Standard answer to 'how are you?' in Pakistan.
Said about any future plan.
m. افسوس ہوا = I'm sorry to hear that.

phrases.en: How are you? (polite, to a man)
How are you? (polite, to a woman)
No problem. / You're welcome. / Never mind.

grammar.title: Word order: the verb comes last
grammar.body:
Urdu is a **subject–object–verb (SOV)** language. Where English says 'I drink tea', Urdu says 'I tea drink': میں چائے پیتا ہوں. The verb (often followed by a form of 'to be', like ہوں / ہے / ہیں) normally ends the sentence.

Even simple 'X is Y' sentences put the verb last: 'I fine am' — میں ٹھیک ہوں. Question words and the word نہیں (not) usually go just before the verb.

Written sentences end with **۔** (the Urdu full stop) and questions with **؟** (a reversed question mark).

examples.en: I am fine. (lit. I fine am)
This is tea. (lit. this tea is)
I'm not well. (نہیں before the verb)

grammar.title: Three ways to say 'you': آپ, تم, تو
grammar.body:
Urdu has three pronouns for 'you', and each takes its own verb form:

**آپ** āp — polite/respectful. Use it with strangers, elders, teachers, customers, in-laws, and anyone you're unsure about. Verb: **ہیں** haiṃ. This is your default.
**تم** tum — familiar. Friends of your own age, younger siblings, children. Verb: **ہو** ho.
**تو** tū — intimate. Very close friends (and only if they use it with you), small children, God in prayer. Used to strangers it is insulting.

Respect also spreads to the rest of the sentence: to an elder you'd say جی ہاں rather than ہاں, and add جی or صاحب after names.

dialogue.title: New neighbours
dialogue.setting: Bilal meets his new neighbour, Mrs Sana, on the stairs of their building in Lahore.

lines.speaker: Bilal
lines.native: الحمد للہ، میں ٹھیک ہوں۔ اور آپ؟
lines.roman: alhamdulillāh, maiṃ ṭhīk hūṃ. aur āp?

lines.speaker: Sana
lines.native: میں بھی ٹھیک ہوں، شکریہ۔ خوش آمدید!
lines.roman: maiṃ bhī ṭhīk hūṃ, shukriya. xush āmdīd!

lines.speaker: Bilal
lines.native: بہت شکریہ۔ آپ سے مل کر خوشی ہوئی۔
lines.roman: bahut shukriya. āp se mil kar xushī hu’ī.
lines.en: Thank you very much. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: Bilal
lines.native: معاف کیجیے، مجھے دیر ہو رہی ہے۔
lines.roman: muʿāf kījiye, mujhe der ho rahī hai.

culture: In Pakistan, السلام علیکم is used by everyone to everyone; the younger or arriving person usually greets first. Men often shake hands (with the right hand, sometimes both hands) and close friends hug; between men and women, wait to see if a hand is offered — a nod with the right hand on the chest is a warm, safe alternative. **جی** is the magic word of Urdu politeness: use it to answer the phone, to say yes, and after names (امی جی، احمد جی). In India, آداب and نمستے are also used by Urdu speakers depending on the company.
